_comment: The specification for field-level copy merge, shared by three implementations:
rekordo-frontend, rekordo-mobile and the Java backend.
Hand-authored on purpose. If this were generated from one implementation, that
implementation's bugs would become the contract. Every case here is a decision
someone made, not an output someone recorded.
Each case is asserted three ways: merge(local, remote) equals expected,
merge(remote, local) equals expected (commutative), and merging the result
against either input again is a no-op (idempotent).
Clocks are encoded as wall:counter:node, fixed width, so lexicographic order
as ONE field. As a source column beside an id column the two would merge under
separate clocks, and one device's source could pair with another's id.
A copy typed in by hand carries the pressing's own facts (manualTitle, manualArtist,
manualYear, manualLabel, manualCatalogNumber, manualFormat) beside its releaseId,
which is "local:<the copy's own id>". They are six mergeable fields rather than one
blob so that correcting the year on one device and the label on another keeps both.

cases.name: different fields edited on each device — both edits survive
same field, same millisecond and counter — the node id breaks the tie
delete on one device, later edit on the other — the edit wins and the copy lives
created on two devices at different times — the earlier creation is the true one
notes edited on both devices — the later wins, the other is kept for the person to reconcile

local.notes: Sleeve is sharp, no seam splits.

expected.notesConflict: Sleeve is sharp, no seam splits.

cases.name: notes changed on one device only — plain last-write-wins, no marker
identical notes on both devices — no conflict, no marker
media regraded on one device, sleeve on the other — both grades survive
catalogue art starred on one device, hidden later on the other — the later choice wins
a hand-entered pressing, corrected on two devices — the title on one, the year on the other
the same hand-entered pressing regraded as vinyl on the later device — the later format wins
the shelf arranged on two devices — the later drag places the record
cases.comment: Arranging renumbers every copy densely, so two people dragging at once produce two complete orders rather than two fractional insertions. Field-level last-write-wins then resolves per copy, and the worst case is one device's whole order winning — an order somebody actually built — instead of an interleaving neither of them meant.
